title: Leadership Communication Lessons From Ted Lasso
summary: This video breaks down leadership communication through scenes from Ted Lasso, showing how great leaders pay attention to quieter team members, help them build self-belief, navigate emotional journeys, and set clear boundaries. The main lesson is that effective motivation requires psychological safety combined with clear leadership boundaries rather than just being nice.
key_points: Pay attention to everyone's potential, especially quieter members who don't put themselves forward.
Help others gain confidence and self-belief by putting the judgment back in their hands and asking questions like "Do you think this will work?".
Take people through the emotional journey from where they are (e.g., fear, envy, shame) to where you want them to be (hope, confidence, belief).
Create psychological safety so people feel safe to speak, question, disagree, fail, and learn.
Psychological safety must come with clear boundaries; a leader must not accept their authority being disrespected.
Meet your audience where they are emotionally before trying to move them forward.
content:
The creator, Shannon Jenkins (leadership communication expert), introduces the analysis of leadership communication using examples from the TV series "Ted Lasso." She states that while Ted Lasso appears to succeed because he is nice, closer observation reveals a far more effective leadership communication style.

Technique 1: Pay Attention to Everyone's Potential
- Good leaders pay attention to everyone on their team, especially those who speak less or don't put themselves forward.
- In the show, Nate is the kitman at the bottom of the hierarchy despite having exceptional knowledge of football tactics.
- When Nate downplays his own tactical idea ("Oh, it's not even very good... it's probably really bad... it's embarrassing"), many leaders would respond with reassurance ("Oh, come on Nate, don't be embarrassed").
- Ted uses a more effective communication tool: he asks a question, "Do you think this will work?"
- This puts the judgment back in Nate's hands, letting him find his own belief in the idea.
- Ted listens seriously, and when Nate finally says yes, Ted gives immediate feedback: "Let's give it a shot."
- The creator explains that when leaders ask people for ideas and never use them or use them without acknowledging the contributor, they damage confidence or create resentment.
- Ted pays attention to the quieter people in the room, invites them in, and creates opportunities to step up—a tactic known as "psychological safety."

Technique 2: Help Others Gain Confidence & Self-Belief
- Ted has spotted both the potential and the limitation in Nate, and he creates conditions for Nate to step forward.
- In a later scene, journalist Trent Crimm asks Ted if the tactical idea was his. Ted replies: "Oh no, no, no. That's all cooked up by our very own Nate the Great... He's Nate the Greats."
- The creator emphasizes the power of that nickname: Nate sees himself as an insignificant kitman whose ideas aren't worth hearing, but Ted repeatedly reflects a different identity back to him ("Nate the Great"), someone whose ideas have value and who belongs in the conversation.

Technique 3: Take People Through the Emotional Journey
- In Season 3, Richmond is in the Premier League, but things are falling apart. Their superstar Zava has just announced his retirement, team morale and confidence are low, and Ted needs to change how they see what happens next.
- Ted enters the locker room, takes down the "BELIEVE" sign, tears it apart piece by piece, and throws it in the bin.
- He tells the team: "It's just a sign. I agree... Believe don't just happen because you hang something up on a wall... It comes from in here... and up here... and down here. Only problem is we all got so much junk floating through us, a lot of times we end up getting in our own way. You know, crap like envy, or fear, shame... I don't want to mess around with that anymore... You know what I want to mess around with? The belief that I matter... regardless of what I do or don't achieve... Or the belief that we all deserve to be loved... Or what about the belief of hope? Yeah, that's what I want to mess around with. Believing that things can get better.
- The creator notes the deliberate journey in those few lines: "I matter," "I can change," "we can change."
- The emotional path moves from disappointment and frustration towards confidence and possibility.
- A leader must not stand on one side of the gap shouting "Hey, come and join me," but walk the whole way with them, giving people a reason to believe in their own ability to influence what happens next.

Technique 4: Create Psychological Safety With Clear Boundaries
- Psychological safety must come with clear boundaries, otherwise it can lead to bad behavior, lack of respect, and oversharing.
- In Season 4, Alice is one of Ted's coaches. She is intense and demanding, and after becoming frustrated with the team, she starts taking her frustration out on the players directly.
- Ted has already told her she cannot do this in his usual benevolent storytelling style, but Alice doesn't listen.
- Ted confronts her directly: "I'm pretty sure I encouraged you to take it a little easier on our team, didn't I?... This game was so much bigger than that. This was their chance to make a statement... Unfortunately, I didn't notice what was going on with him before he'd been burned to a crisp. So in the hopes of learning from my mistakes, I'm going to try a different approach with you... I'm going to suspend you for a match."
- Alice replies that there's only one match left before the Christmas break. Ted responds: "Maybe that'll give you some time to think about what's going on... make some adjustments, and hopefully we'll see you in the new year."
- The creator points out that Alice chose to directly challenge Ted's authority, so he changed his communication, and the consequence was clear: "I'm going to suspend you for a match."
- Ted is kind—he cares about others, gives everyone a voice, motivates, listens, and encourages initiative—but he does not accept his authority being disrespected.
- Ted's communication of the consequence involves no humiliation, anger, or long lecture; he is clear, firm, and still manages to be warm with her, which is a rare and difficult combination.
creator: Shannon Jenkins
